patient.name: Kwame Mensah
patient.complaint: Three days of severe throbbing pain beside the anus, worse on sitting
background: Type 2 diabetes for 10 years, on metformin and gliclazide
Bus driver in Lewisham; sits for long shifts

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with acute throbbing perianal pain, fever and a fluctuant swelling (abscess), or chronic discharge from an opening beside the anus (fistula). Diarrhoea and weight loss point to Crohn's.

points: Kwame, 46, has had **throbbing pain** beside his anus for 3 days.
He **cannot sit** through his bus shift.
Since last night: fevers, sweats and feeling generally unwell.
No rectal bleeding; bowels open normally.

steps.lead: Acute pain plus fever beside the anus means an **acute pus collection**: an abscess. In most people, like Kwame, the source is an infected anal gland.
Kwame has had diabetes for **10 years**, exactly the long-standing diabetes that raises susceptibility.

visual.title: Kwame's HbA1c
visual.label: Kwame 76
visual.caption: Poor control impairs immunity and wound healing, so abscesses form more easily and heal more slowly.

points: Left of the anal verge: a **hot, red, tender, fluctuant** swelling.
Surrounding skin red and indurated: early **cellulitis**.
No external opening or discharge seen.
Rectal examination is too painful to tolerate.

steps.lead: Kwame has the **abscess** picture: acute, throbbing, fluctuant, febrile, unable to sit. A fistula would instead give chronic discharge and underwear staining.

steps.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis for Kwame now?
steps.r: Fever plus a **tender fluctuant swelling** beside the anal verge is a perianal abscess. A pilonidal abscess sits in the natal cleft, away from the anus.

steps.title: Abscess or fistula?
head: Perianal abscess
Anal fistula
rows: Abnormal tract, anal canal to skin

steps.lead: Kwame's **previous abscess** two years ago matters: if a collection is not fully drained, it can leave a fistula behind.

steps.q: Which extra history matters most before labelling this simple cryptoglandular disease?
steps.r: Recurrent perianal sepsis with **diarrhoea and weight loss** suggests Crohn's disease. Kwame has neither.

steps.lead: Kwame's bowels are normal and his weight is steady, so Crohn's is less likely, but his recurrence keeps it on the list.

steps.text: A **thrombosed haemorrhoid** is a tender purple lump at the anal margin, but it is not fluctuant and does not cause fever. A **fissure** gives sharp pain on defecation with bright red blood.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' A simple abscess is diagnosed clinically; recurrent, deep or complex disease needs MRI pelvis, and the gold standard for a fistula is MRI pelvis plus examination under anaesthesia (EUA).

steps.q: Kwame has an obvious fluctuant perianal abscess. Does he need imaging before drainage?
steps.r: A superficial, obvious abscess is diagnosed on **history and examination**. Imaging is kept for deep, unclear, recurrent or complex disease.

steps.lead: Kwame's abscess is superficial and obvious, so no imaging is needed now. If he later develops a fistula, **MRI pelvis plus EUA** maps it.

steps.title: Kwame's bloods in ED
steps.text: Raised WCC and CRP show a systemic response. High glucose with normal ketones: **hyperglycaemia without DKA**, which drainage and insulin will improve.

visual.title: White cell count
visual.label: Kwame 15.9
visual.caption: A raised WCC plus fever and cellulitis are the **systemic features** that mean antibiotics are added to drainage.

steps.title: Which perianal test, when?
nodes: Clinical diagnosis: straight to incision and drainage
Deep, unclear, recurrent or complex disease
steps.caption: MRI maps the tract against the sphincters; EUA lets the surgeon find the internal opening directly.

steps.text: Always check the **capillary glucose** (and ketones if high) in a perianal abscess. Poorly controlled diabetes is both a cause and a complication of the sepsis.
Do not pick **CT** or **colonoscopy** to map a fistula. CT is for suspected deep pelvic sepsis when MRI is unavailable; colonoscopy looks for Crohn's, not the tract.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' The answer for an abscess is urgent incision and drainage (antibiotics only added for cellulitis or systemic features). A fistula needs referral to colorectal/General Surgery for fistulotomy or seton.

steps.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of Kwame's abscess?
steps.r: Pus must be let out: **incision and drainage** is both the initial and the definitive treatment. Antibiotics alone do not penetrate a collection.

steps.lead: Kwame has cellulitis, fever and a raised WCC, so he gets **antibiotics added** to his incision and drainage.

points: Incision and drainage under general anaesthetic; 20 mL of pus drained.
Cavity left open to drain and heal from the base.
IV antibiotics for the cellulitis; insulin sliding scale for glucose.
Pus sent for culture: mixed bowel flora.

visual.title: After drainage
visual.caption: Once the pus is out, CRP and glucose fall together. A CRP that keeps rising suggests a residual collection.

points: Persistent **discharge** and staining of his underwear.
An **external opening** 2 cm from the anal verge at 4 o'clock.
No pain or fever now; no diarrhoea or weight loss.

steps.q: Which is the most appropriate next step for Kwame's suspected fistula?
steps.r: An anal fistula needs **specialist surgical** assessment (MRI pelvis + EUA) and an operation. Antibiotics and GTN do not close a tract.

steps.lead: Kwame's MRI shows a low tract through little sphincter muscle, so the surgeon plans a **fistulotomy**. A higher tract would get a **seton**.

steps.title: Fistula operations
head: Fistulotomy
Seton
rows: Lay the tract open to heal from base
Prolonged treatment, may need later surgery

steps.lead: UK guidance (NICE CKS and ACPGBI) frames Kwame's care: drain abscesses urgently, refer fistulas to colorectal surgeons.

steps.text: **Antibiotics never replace drainage.** In the exam, 'oral antibiotics and outpatient follow-up' for a fluctuant perianal swelling is always wrong.

science.exam: Expect an applied mechanism: blocked anal crypt glands at the dentate line (cryptoglandular), transmural inflammation in Crohn's, or Goodsall's rule predicting the internal opening.

steps.title: From anal gland to fistula
nodes: Anal crypt gland at the dentate line blocks
Pus collects in intersphincteric, ischiorectal or supralevator space
Chronic fistula, anal canal to skin
steps.caption: Abscess and fistula are the acute and chronic ends of the same cryptoglandular process.

steps.lead: Kwame's abscess began in an **anal crypt gland**, then pus tracked into the spaces around the sphincters.
His first abscess two years ago probably left a tract that **epithelialised**, which is why it kept discharging.

steps.q: Kwame's external opening is posterior to the transverse anal line. By Goodsall's rule, where is the internal opening likely to be?
o: Directly opposite in a straight line
Within the rectum above the levators
steps.r: **Goodsall's rule:** posterior openings follow a curved tract to the **posterior midline**; anterior openings run straight, radially, into the canal.

steps.lead: If Kwame had Crohn's, **transmural** inflammation could create tracts anywhere, giving complex, recurrent fistulas.
Kwame's poorly controlled diabetes weakened local defence, helping both abscesses form and slowing healing.

steps.text: **Ulcerative colitis** is mucosal only, so it rarely causes fistulas. Transmural inflammation is why fistulas point to **Crohn's**.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of a perianal abscess?
mcq.r: Most abscesses and fistulas come from **infected anal glands** (cryptoglandular).

mcq.q: Which feature most suggests an anal fistula rather than an abscess?
o: Persistent discharge from an external opening
mcq.r: A fistula is **chronic**: recurrent discharge and staining from an opening near the anus.

mcq.q: Recurrent perianal fistulas with diarrhoea and weight loss suggest which condition?
mcq.r: **Crohn's** causes transmural inflammation, so tracts form.

mcq.q: What is the main complication of an inadequately drained perianal abscess?
mcq.r: Persistent infection can track and **epithelialise into a fistula**.

mcq.q: How is a simple superficial perianal abscess usually diagnosed?
mcq.r: History and examination are enough; imaging is for deep, recurrent or complex disease.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard assessment of an anal fistula?
mcq.r: **MRI pelvis + examination under anaesthesia** is the gold-standard combination.

mcq.q: What is the initial and definitive treatment of a perianal abscess?
When are antibiotics added to drainage of a perianal abscess?
mcq.r: Add antibiotics for surrounding **cellulitis** or **systemic infection**.

mcq.q: Where do the anal glands that cause cryptoglandular abscesses open?
mcq.r: Anal crypt glands open at the **dentate line**.

prompts.q: What is the difference between a perianal abscess and an anal fistula, and what usually causes both?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: acute pus versus chronic tract, same root cause.

points.p: Abscess = acute collection of pus
points.why: Acute, painful and fluctuant.

points.p: Fistula = chronic abnormal tract (anal canal to perianal skin)
points.why: Chronic discharge rather than acute pain.

points.p: Most common cause is cryptoglandular infection (anal glands)
points.why: Crohn's is a less common cause.

points.p: Persistent or recurrent discharge (intermittent pus)

points.p: External opening near the anus
points.why: The external end of the tract.

points.p: Staining of underwear and local irritation
points.why: Often presents as pruritus ani.

points.p: Recurrent abscesses

points.p: Long-standing diabetes mellitus
points.why: Impaired immunity and wound healing.

prompts.q: Which features should make you suspect Crohn's disease in perianal sepsis?

points.p: Recurrent fistulas or perianal sepsis
points.why: Multiple or complex tracts are typical.

prompts.q: How is perianal disease investigated, and what is the gold standard for a fistula?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: simple abscess needs no imaging; complex disease does.

points.p: Simple abscess: clinical diagnosis (history and examination)
points.why: Do not delay drainage for imaging.

points.p: Deep, unclear, recurrent or complex: MRI pelvis
points.why: MRI shows tracts against the sphincters.

points.p: Fistula gold standard: MRI pelvis plus EUA
points.why: The combination, not either alone.

points.p: Check glucose (and ketones) in diabetics
points.why: Sepsis worsens diabetic control.

prompts.q: How is a perianal abscess managed, and when are antibiotics added?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the answer is drainage; antibiotics are only an add-on.

points.p: Incision and drainage: initial and definitive
points.why: Urgent; antibiotics alone are wrong.

points.p: Add antibiotics for surrounding cellulitis
points.why: Redness spreading beyond the collection.

points.p: Add antibiotics for systemic infection features
points.why: Fever, tachycardia, raised WCC.

prompts.q: How is an anal fistula managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: it is a surgical problem; refer.

points.p: Specialist referral to colorectal or General Surgery
points.why: Especially if it presents with an abscess.

points.p: Fistulotomy for low simple tracts
points.why: Lays the tract open; risk to continence if high.

points.p: Seton for high or complex tracts
points.why: Drains and protects the sphincter; used in Crohn's.

prompts.q: Why do perianal abscesses form and why do fistulas develop?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one process from gland to tract.

points.p: Anal crypt glands at the dentate line become obstructed and infected
points.why: The cryptoglandular theory.

points.p: Pus collects in intersphincteric, ischiorectal or supralevator spaces
points.why: These spaces name the abscess type.

points.p: Inadequately drained abscess tracks and epithelialises into a fistula
points.why: Lining forms, so the tract persists.

points.p: Goodsall's rule predicts the internal opening from the external one
points.why: Posterior openings curve to the posterior midline.

prompts.q: Why does Crohn's disease cause fistulas, and why do diabetes and immunosuppression raise risk?

points.p: Crohn's inflammation is transmural (full thickness)
points.why: UC is mucosal, so rarely fistulates.

points.p: Diabetes and immunosuppression impair local immune defence
points.why: More likely to form.

points.p: They also impair wound healing
points.why: Slower to resolve.

glossary.Perianal abscess: An acute collection of pus in the tissues around the anus.
glossary.Anal fistula: A chronic abnormal tract connecting the anal canal to the perianal skin.
glossary.Fistula-in-ano: Another name for an anal fistula.
glossary.Cryptoglandular: Arising from the anal glands that open into the anal crypts at the dentate line.
glossary.Anal crypt: A small pocket in the anal canal lining at the dentate line, where anal glands open.
glossary.Dentate line: The wavy line in the anal canal marking the junction of hindgut and ectoderm-derived epithelium.
glossary.Anal verge: The outer edge of the anal canal where it meets perianal skin.
glossary.Fluctuant: Feels like a fluid-filled swelling that shifts on pressure, suggesting pus.
glossary.Cellulitis: Spreading bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, causing redness, warmth and swelling.
glossary.Induration: Firm, thickened tissue caused by inflammation.
glossary.Erythema: Redness of the skin from increased blood flow.
glossary.Intersphincteric: The space between the internal and external anal sphincters.
glossary.Ischiorectal: The fat-filled space beside the anal canal, between the levator ani and the ischium.
glossary.Supralevator: The space above the levator ani muscles; abscesses here are deep and hard to see.
glossary.Epithelialise: Become lined with epithelium, which makes a tract permanent.
glossary.Goodsall's rule: Predicts the internal fistula opening: posterior external openings curve to the posterior midline, anterior ones run straight.
glossary.Transmural: Through the full thickness of the bowel wall, typical of Crohn's disease.
glossary.Crohn's disease: Inflammatory bowel disease with patchy transmural inflammation anywhere from mouth to anus.
glossary.Ulcerative colitis: Inflammatory bowel disease with continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon, rarely causing fistulas.
glossary.EUA: Examination under anaesthesia: the surgeon examines and probes the anal canal while the patient is asleep.
glossary.MRI pelvis: Magnetic resonance imaging that maps abscesses and fistula tracts against the sphincters.
glossary.Incision and drainage: Cutting open an abscess to let the pus out; the definitive treatment.
glossary.Fistulotomy: Laying the fistula tract open so it heals from the base.
glossary.Seton: A thread or band passed through a fistula tract to keep it draining and protect the sphincter.
glossary.Pilonidal abscess: An abscess in the natal cleft from infected hair follicles, not related to the anus.
glossary.Thrombosed haemorrhoid: A haemorrhoid containing clot: a painful purple lump at the anal margin, without fever.
glossary.Anal fissure: A tear in the anal canal lining causing sharp pain and bleeding on defecation.
glossary.Fournier's gangrene: A rapidly spreading necrotising infection of the perineum; a surgical emergency.
glossary.HbA1c: Glycated haemoglobin, showing average blood glucose control over about 3 months.
glossary.Faecal calprotectin: A stool marker of bowel inflammation, raised in inflammatory bowel disease.
glossary.Infliximab: An anti-TNF antibody used to treat Crohn's disease, including fistulating disease.
glossary.ACPGBI: Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland, which issues colorectal surgery guidance.
glossary.NICE CKS: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: short UK guidance for primary care.
glossary.Sitz bath: Sitting in warm shallow water to soothe the perianal area.

practice.e: A simple perianal abscess is usually diagnosed clinically; MRI pelvis is for deep, unclear, recurrent or complex disease.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show for this patient.
An obvious, superficial first abscess in a well woman.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Simple perianal abscess is diagnosed **clinically**; no imaging needed.

elim: Unnecessary radiation for an obvious superficial abscess.
Too painful, and not needed for an obvious collection.
Used with MRI for fistulas, not to diagnose a simple abscess.
Kept for deep, unclear, recurrent or complex disease.

steps.x: **A. Clinical history and examination.** Obvious superficial abscess = clinical diagnosis, straight to drainage.

practice.stem: A 39 year old man has a 3 day history of severe perianal pain. There is a tender, fluctuant swelling beside the anus. He has no other medical problems. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 130/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Incision and drainage is the initial and definitive management of a perianal abscess. Oral antibiotics alone do not clear pus.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now.

clues: tender, fluctuant swelling beside the anus
steps.x: A fluctuant collection beside the anus: a perianal abscess.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Initial and definitive treatment: **incision and drainage**.

elim: Treats a fistula, not an acute abscess.
Soothes fissures or haemorrhoids; it leaves the pus in.
Antibiotics do not treat a collection and risk fistula formation.
A treatment for anal fissure.

steps.x: **A. Incision and drainage.** Fluctuant = drain it.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has a large perianal abscess with spreading redness and induration across the left buttock. She feels unwell and shivery. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 114 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Incision and drainage is the treatment; antibiotics are added because of surrounding cellulitis and systemic features. Antibiotics alone never replace drainage.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now.
Abscess plus surrounding cellulitis and systemic infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Drain the abscess and **add antibiotics** for the cellulitis and sepsis.

elim: Enough for a simple abscess, but she has cellulitis and systemic features.
Antibiotics cannot clear the pus; drainage is still needed.
Delays source control in a septic patient.
For a fistula, not an acute abscess.

steps.x: **B. Incision and drainage with antibiotics.** Cellulitis or systemic features = drainage plus antibiotics.

practice.stem: A 42 year old man has an 8 month history of intermittent pus discharge from an opening beside his anus, after an abscess was drained last year. He has no bowel symptoms. His GP has given two courses of antibiotics without benefit. His temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 70 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: An anal fistula needs specialist colorectal surgical input (MRI + EUA, then fistulotomy or seton). Antibiotics do not close a tract; infliximab is for Crohn's.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs right now.

clues: two courses of antibiotics without benefit
steps.x: Chronic discharge from an opening after an abscess: a cryptoglandular fistula.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A fistula needs **specialist surgery** (fistulotomy or seton): refer to colorectal surgery.

elim: Antibiotics do not close an epithelialised tract.
A fistula will not heal on its own.
For fistulating Crohn's; he has no bowel symptoms.
A treatment for anal fissure.

steps.x: **D. Referral to colorectal surgery.** A fistula is a surgical problem: refer.

practice.stem: A 35 year old man has a perianal abscess drained. The surgeon explains that most such abscesses start inside the anal canal and spread outwards into the tissues around the sphincters. His temperature is 37.8°C and pulse rate 96 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his abscess?
o: Bacterial invasion of a hair follicle in the natal cleft
Infection of an obstructed anal crypt gland at the dentate line
Rupture of a thrombosed external haemorrhoid
Transmural granulomatous inflammation of the rectum
practice.e: Cryptoglandular infection: anal crypt glands at the dentate line block and become infected, and pus spreads into the intersphincteric, ischiorectal or supralevator spaces.

steps.x: A science question: link the clinical picture to its mechanism.

clues: spread outwards into the tissues around the sphincters
steps.x: Starts in the anal canal, spreads into the perianal spaces.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **cryptoglandular** mechanism: a blocked, infected anal gland at the dentate line.

elim: This is pilonidal disease.
Causes ischaemic proctitis, not perianal abscess.
Causes bleeding, not a deep collection.
Crohn's mechanism; he has no features of Crohn's.

steps.x: **B. Infection of an obstructed anal crypt gland at the dentate line.** Most abscesses = blocked anal crypt gland at the dentate line.
